title: "Federated similarity search"

```{python}
#| include: false
import os

os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "2")
```

## The use case

A clinician has an unusual case and wants to ask a network of hospitals
whether anyone has seen patients like it. Each hospital holds
embeddings of its own patients, produced by a model it fine-tuned
privately. Nobody will share embeddings, and nobody will share a model.

There are two obstacles, and only one of them is cryptographic.

The **geometric** obstacle: embeddings from different fine-tunes do not
live in a shared space. An inner product between a query from the
public base model and a hospital's privately fine-tuned embedding is
not a similarity — it is a comparison between two different coordinate
systems.

The **cryptographic** obstacle: the query must not be readable by any
hospital, the databases must not be readable by anyone, and no single
party may be able to decrypt.

## The adapter

Each site fixes the geometry locally. A public *anchor cohort* is
published; each site embeds it with its own fine-tuned model, and then
fits the orthogonal map that best carries the public geometry onto its
own. That map is the site's **compatibility adapter**, and it never
leaves the site.

Orthogonality is doing real work here. An orthogonal map preserves
inner products, so moving the query into a site's coordinates leaves
the similarity unchanged. A general linear map would stretch some
directions and shrink others, and the number that came back would no
longer be a cosine.

The direction also matters, and it is easy to get backwards: the
adapter is applied to the *incoming query*, so it must map public
coordinates to site coordinates. The database stays where it is.

```{python}
import numpy as np
from homomorphepy.examples.similarity import simulate, fit_adapter

anchor_public, sites = simulate()
adapter = fit_adapter(anchor_public, sites[0]["anchor_site"])

# The adapter should reproduce the site's own anchor embeddings from
# the public ones. This site's fine-tune is an orthogonal drift, so an
# orthogonal adapter can undo it exactly.
float(np.max(np.abs(adapter @ anchor_public.T - sites[0]["anchor_site"].T)))
```

## Doing it under encryption

The query is encrypted under a joint key held by no one. Two operations
then have to happen while it stays encrypted, and both are built from
*rotations* of the encrypted vector's slots.

**Applying the adapter.** A matrix times an encrypted vector is
computed from the matrix's generalized diagonals:

$$A\,q \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} d_i \odot \mathrm{rot}(q, i).$$

Each term multiplies the encrypted vector by an *unencrypted* diagonal.
That is cheaper than multiplying two encrypted quantities, and the
whole product costs a single level of the precision budget.

**The inner product.** Multiplying slot-wise by the site's own
unencrypted database vector, then folding the slots together by
repeated rotate-and-add, leaves the similarity in slot 0 — in
$\log_2 p$ rotations rather than $p$.

Under threshold keys, rotation keys cannot come from a secret key,
because no secret key exists. They are built by an $n$-of-$n$ ceremony
that mirrors the one that built the public key:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from homomorphepy.actors import make_joint_rotation_keys

make_joint_rotation_keys(master, range(1, p))
```

## The whole protocol

```{python}
from homomorphepy.examples.similarity import run

r = run()
print(f"{r.n_candidates} candidates across 3 sites, embedding width {r.p}")
for name, i, score in r.top_k:
    print(f"  {name} patient {i}: {score:.6f}")
```

Nothing above was decrypted except the final scores, and those only
through the $n$-of-$n$ ceremony. The aggregator saw encrypted values
throughout.

## Does it give the right answer?

The protocol is only worth anything if it returns what the same search
would have returned in the clear.

```{python}
print(f"max score error vs cleartext : {r.max_abs_score_error:.2e}")
print(f"identical ranking            : {r.rank_agreement}")
```

The scores agree to CKKS approximation error, and the ranking — which
is what a user actually consumes — is identical.

## Does the adapter have to be orthogonal?

Everything above runs at the orthogonal endpoint, where the adapter
inverts the drift exactly and the score is a true cosine. But real
fine-tuning is not orthogonal. A site that trains freely stretches some
directions more than others, and no rotation can undo that.

So relax the constraint. Fit the adapter by minimizing

$$\lVert Z_{\text{site}} A - Z_{\text{public}}\rVert^2
  \;+\; \mu \lVert A^\top A - I\rVert^2,$$

where $\mu \to \infty$ forces orthogonality (the Procrustes solution
used above), $\mu = 0$ is unconstrained least squares, and values in
between give near-orthogonal maps.

These sweeps run **in the clear**. The encrypted and unencrypted scores
agree to $10^{-13}$, so running them through encryption would cost
hours and change no digit — and what is being asked here is a
statistical question, not a cryptographic one.

```{python}
from homomorphepy.examples.similarity import mu_sweep
import pandas as pd

s = mu_sweep()
pd.DataFrame(s["table"]).assign(
    ideal=s["ideal"], unaligned=s["unaligned"], gram=s["gram"]
).round(3)
```

Three things fall out.

**Alignment is not optional.** Without an adapter, recall collapses to
`{python} round(s["unaligned"], 3)` against an achievable
`{python} round(s["ideal"], 3)` — no better than guessing. The
geometric obstacle is the whole problem; the encryption is the easy
part.

**The two deployments coincide only at the orthogonal endpoint.** At
$\mu = \infty$ the Design 1 and Design 2 columns are identical, exactly
as the algebra says they must be: an orthogonal map preserves norms, so
folding it into the database and applying it to the query are the same
operation. At finite $\mu$ they separate, and folding wins — because
the renormalization it performs repairs some of the distortion the
non-orthogonal map introduces.

**An intermediate $\mu$ beats both endpoints.** The rigid endpoint
gives up recall it does not need to; unconstrained least squares
distorts the geometry more than it repairs. Neither extreme is the
right default.

Now vary the drift itself. $\beta$ is the non-isometry magnitude:
$\beta = 0$ is an exactly orthogonal fine-tune, and larger values
stretch directions increasingly unevenly.

```{python}
from homomorphepy.examples.similarity import beta_sweep

pd.DataFrame(beta_sweep()).round(3)
```

At $\beta = 0$ the orthogonal adapter matches the ideal exactly — it
inverts an orthogonal drift perfectly, which is the sanity check that
the machinery is right. As $\beta$ grows the rigid adapter falls away
while the relaxed one holds. That is the practical finding: **the more
freely a site fine-tunes, the more the orthogonality constraint costs
you**, and a deployment facing genuinely free fine-tuning should not
default to Procrustes.

The convex Gram alternative is included in the first table for
comparison. It is analytic and therefore attractive, and it performs
close to no alignment at all.

## What this does not do

**Top-$k$ selection happens in the clear.** The aggregator decrypts
every candidate score and then sorts. Selecting the top $k$ *under*
encryption is possible in CKKS via polynomial sign approximation, but
it costs depth and complexity out of proportion to what it adds here.
The consequence is that the aggregator learns every score, not only the
$k$ it returns.

**Patient indices travel in the clear** alongside the encrypted scores,
so the aggregator learns which site holds a match and at which local
position, though not who that patient is.

**Repeated adaptive queries leak.** A querier who submits many chosen
embeddings learns about the shape of the cohort. That is a property of
any retrieval system that returns real answers, and encryption does not
address it; query budgets do.

**The trust model is honest-but-curious.** A site that misreports its
scores can corrupt the ranking undetected. Catching that needs
verifiable computation, which this does not attempt.

**One encrypted value per patient.** At this scale that is fine. A
production deployment would pack many patients into the slots of a
single encrypted value and amortize both the adapter and the reduction
across them.
